entries.name: Maximum groundspeed
entries.evidence: (a) The groundspeed of the small unmanned aircraft may not exceed 87 knots (100 miles per hour).
entries.note: The single figure, both units as printed: 87 knots / 100 mph.

entries.name: Maximum altitude above ground level
entries.evidence: (b) The altitude of the small unmanned aircraft cannot be higher than 400 feet above ground level, unless the small unmanned aircraft: (1) Is flown within a 400-foot radius of a structure; and (2) Does not fly higher than 400 feet above the structure's immediate uppermost limit.
entries.note: 400 feet, and the 400-foot structure radius and 400-foot above-structure allowance as three distinct figures.

entries.name: Minimum flight visibility
entries.evidence: (c) The minimum flight visibility, as observed from the location of the control station must be no less than 3 statute miles. For purposes of this section, flight visibility means the average slant distance from the control station at which prominent unlighted objects may be seen and identified by day and prominent lighted objects may be seen and identified by night.
entries.note: 3 statute miles, plus the section's own definition of flight visibility, which is a definition and not a threshold. The figure is fixed and this entry states it, which is why it stays clear; the definition it quotes turns on 'prominent', which the corpus never fixes, and that is prominent-objects — carried by the entry that applies the definition rather than by the one that states the figure.

entries.name: Minimum distance from clouds
entries.evidence: (d) The minimum distance of the small unmanned aircraft from clouds must be no less than: (1) 500 feet below the cloud; and (2) 2,000 feet horizontally from the cloud.
entries.note: Both figures: 500 ft below, 2,000 ft horizontal. A single combined value would lose the distinction.

entries.name: Civil twilight, outside Alaska
entries.evidence: (1) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins 30 minutes before official sunrise and ends at official sunrise; (2) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins at official sunset and ends 30 minutes after official sunset;
entries.note: Both windows: 30 minutes before official sunrise to sunrise, and sunset to 30 minutes after.

entries.name: Groundspeed is within the limit
entries.evidence: (a) The groundspeed of the small unmanned aircraft may not exceed 87 knots (100 miles per hour).
entries.note: At, just below and just above 87 knots. The printed mph figure is a rounding of the knots figure; test which one governs.

entries.name: Altitude is within the limit
entries.evidence: (b) The altitude of the small unmanned aircraft cannot be higher than 400 feet above ground level, unless the small unmanned aircraft: (1) Is flown within a 400-foot radius of a structure; and (2) Does not fly higher than 400 feet above the structure's immediate uppermost limit.
entries.note: The plain 400 ft AGL case; inside a 400 ft radius of a structure; and the boundary where the aircraft is within the radius but above the structure's uppermost limit plus 400.

entries.name: Visibility and cloud clearance are met
entries.evidence: (c) The minimum flight visibility, as observed from the location of the control station must be no less than 3 statute miles. For purposes of this section, flight visibility means the average slant distance from the control station at which prominent unlighted objects may be seen and identified by day and prominent lighted objects may be seen and identified by night. (d) The minimum distance of the small unmanned aircraft from clouds must be no less than: (1) 500 feet below the cloud; and (2) 2,000 feet horizontally from the cloud.
entries.note: Each minimum independently, and the case where one passes and the other fails. The cloud-clearance half is fully computable from two stated figures. The visibility half is not: the quantity to be compared against 3 statute miles is the section's own 'flight visibility', whose definiens turns on which objects are 'prominent', and the corpus fixes no degree of prominence. That term is prominent-objects, split out rather than reclassifying this entry — classifying the whole entry by one of its clauses would have thrown away the 500-foot and 2,000-foot figures (0005).

entries.name: Which objects are prominent, for flight visibility
entries.evidence: For purposes of this section, flight visibility means the average slant distance from the control station at which prominent unlighted objects may be seen and identified by day and prominent lighted objects may be seen and identified by night.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define 'prominent', and the term carries the whole visibility metric: the distance reported as flight visibility is the distance at which prominent objects can be seen, so the degree of prominence fixes the number that § 107.51(c)'s 3-statute-mile threshold is compared against.

entries.note: Gate 1 of 0008 passes: applying § 107.51(c) requires fixing a degree the corpus did not fix, which is what separates flight visibility from groundspeed — an ordinary caller-supplied parameter whose meaning is not open. Gate 2 does not fire: no corpus is named for it. Gate 3's first branch does not fire either — the clause states no measure for 'prominent' in its own constituent and names no decider — so the procedure returns a gap. The same shape as well-clear and moving-vehicle-operation's 'sparsely populated area'. Found by the undefined-term sweep (#33, #34), not by inspection of the interesting entries.

entries.name: Only one aircraft is operated at a time
entries.evidence: A person may not operate or act as a remote pilot in command or visual observer in the operation of more than one unmanned aircraft at the same time.
entries.note: One aircraft; two aircraft; and the same person acting as visual observer for a second. The prohibition binds three roles — operating, acting as remote pilot in command, acting as visual observer — and the evidence covers each. This wording bars a person who may 'operate'; the later wording bars one who may 'manipulate flight controls'.

entries.name: Controlled airspace requires prior ATC authorization
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in Class B, Class C, or Class D airspace or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport unless that person has prior authorization from Air Traffic Control (ATC).
entries.note: Each of Class B, C, D and the lateral surface area of Class E, with and without authorization; and Class G, which needs none. The airspace class is an input. Determining it from a position requires a corpus this map has not admitted.

entries.name: Prohibited or restricted areas require permission
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in prohibited or restricted areas unless that person has permission from the using or controlling agency, as appropriate.
entries.note: Both designations the section states — prohibited and restricted — with and without permission from the using or controlling agency. Same shape as airspace-authorized: the designation is an input, not something derived here.

entries.name: Operation from a moving vehicle or aircraft
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system— (a) From a moving aircraft; or (b) From a moving land or water-borne vehicle unless the small unmanned aircraft is flown over a sparsely populated area and is not transporting another person's property for compensation or hire.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define 'sparsely populated area', and the term carries the whole exception in (b).

entries.note: From a moving aircraft (always prohibited); from a moving land or water-borne vehicle over a sparsely populated area without carriage for hire; and the two ways the exception fails. The summary this note replaces said "a moving land vehicle" and dropped the water-borne case (#26).

entries.name: Night operation is prohibited
entries.evidence: (a) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system during night.
entries.note: There is no condition under which night operation is permitted, and no exception is stated — so the rule is the word 'night' and nothing else, and § 107.3 does not define it: it defines six terms at this date and night is not among them. The engine cannot compute 'night' and not-night; it can only be told. § 107.3 puts § 1.1 of this chapter in force for this part ("if there is a conflict… the definitions in this part control"), so gate 2 of 0008 routes the term to definedElsewhere rather than to a gap, and the whole entry declines. Note that § 107.29(c) fixes civil twilight for purposes of paragraph (b) alone, in the paragraph next door: the drafter fixed the temporal boundary he meant to be computed and left this one to § 1.1. The limit, stated where the claim is: § 107.3's clause is a general priority rule and does not route this term to § 1.1 by name, so the claim that § 1.1 fixes it becomes checkable only when cfr-14-1 is admitted. This entry was recorded as clarity: clear with a computable rule until #33; that verdict and moving-vehicle-operation's rested on identical ground and disagreed.

entries.name: Operation during civil twilight
entries.evidence: (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system during periods of civil twilight unless the small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so. (c) For purposes of paragraph (b) of this section, civil twilight refers to the following: (1) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins 30 minutes before official sunrise and ends at official sunrise; (2) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins at official sunset and ends 30 minutes after official sunset; and (3) In Alaska, the period of civil twilight as defined in the Air Almanac.

crossReferences.cites: as defined in the Air Almanac

entries.note: Inside and outside each twilight window, with and without lighting. Alaska is a separate entry: the corpus defers the definition elsewhere. civil-twilight-alaska is in dependsOn because (c)(3) is part of the definition of civil twilight this entry's rule turns on: (c)(1) and (c)(2) each begin "Except for Alaska", so in Alaska only (c)(3) defines the period, and an Alaskan operation's case resolves only through civil-twilight-alaska, which defers it to the Air Almanac. This map lacked the edge while its own "as defined in the Air Almanac" crossReference already resolved to that entry; the 2026 map's blind second mapping added the edge for the same words (examples/faa-part-107/blind-mapping/ (0014)), and § 107.29(c) reads the same at both dates. (c)'s "paragraph (b) of this section" resolves to anti-collision-lighting, whose locator cites § 107.29(b) and whose evidence quotes all of (b) as it stands at this date, both sentences; intensity-reduction-in-interest-of-safety quotes the second, and this date has no flash-rate clause. The pointer resolves to where (b) is stated; the rule that uses (c)'s definition is this entry's, and anti-collision-lighting does not depend on it.

entries.name: Civil twilight in Alaska
entries.evidence: (3) In Alaska, the period of civil twilight as defined in the Air Almanac.
entries.note: § 107.29(c)(3) fixes the meaning of Alaskan civil twilight in the Air Almanac, which this map has not admitted. Not an ambiguity: the corpus is clear, and the text that would settle it is elsewhere. Nothing beyond the quoted sentence can be evidenced from this corpus.

entries.name: Carriage of hazardous material
entries.evidence: A small unmanned aircraft may not carry hazardous material. For purposes of this section, the term hazardous material is defined in 49 CFR 171.8.
entries.note: § 107.36 states the prohibition here and fixes the meaning of 'hazardous material' in 49 CFR 171.8, which this map has not admitted. Not an ambiguity: the corpus says exactly what it means and says where. Nothing beyond the quoted sentences can be evidenced from this corpus.

entries.name: Yielding right of way to other aircraft
entries.evidence: (a) Each small unmanned aircraft must yield the right of way to all aircraft, airborne vehicles, and launch and reentry vehicles. Yielding the right of way means that the small unmanned aircraft must give way to the aircraft or vehicle and may not pass over, under, or ahead of it unless well clear.
entries.note: Two enumerations, both computable: three protected kinds — aircraft, airborne vehicles, launch and reentry vehicles — and three prohibited relative positions — over, under, ahead. An engine told the object is none of the three, or that the manoeuvre is none of the three, decides the case without the open term at all, and the evidence covers each. The note this replaces said "nothing here is computed", which its own evidence contradicts (#34). What is not computed is the exception "unless well clear", which is well-clear and is a gap rather than an assertion: 0008 § 2 attacked the purpose clause at this joint and it gave way, so gate 3's first branch does not fire here.

entries.name: The small unmanned aircraft is well clear of the aircraft or vehicle
entries.evidence: Yielding the right of way means that the small unmanned aircraft must give way to the aircraft or vehicle and may not pass over, under, or ahead of it unless well clear.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define 'well clear', and the term carries the whole exception to the prohibition on passing over, under or ahead. 'Well clear' occurs exactly once in the corpus; § 107.3 does not define it and no other section does; and § 107.37(a) states no measure for it in its own constituent — 'must give way' is a coordinate obligation in the definiens, not what the clearance is measured against.

entries.note: Split out of right-of-way, which keeps the two computable enumerations (0005: a standard is its own entry, and the rule that consumes it depends on it). Not kind: assertion — gate 3's first branch requires the corpus to state, in the same constituent as the open term, either the measure or the set of values, and § 107.37(a) states neither. Not a value either: the corpus states no clearance. The kind records what the engine would have to do and cannot, which is why the entry declines at runtime rather than demanding a parameter. The same shape as moving-vehicle-operation's 'sparsely populated area', and the two now return the same answer, which they did not before. Where the project holds the term determinate — 'well clear' is a recognised operational standard in aviation practice — that is fate: decision with a record, never a kind (0008 § 3); this map does not hold it, so the fate is unresolved.

entries.name: Operating so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard
entries.evidence: (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard.
entries.note: The corpus states a standard rather than a distance, deliberately, and § 107.37(b) is that sentence and nothing else — so the entry is reclassified in place rather than split. The assertion is asserted and withheld, attributed and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent. An engine that resolved it to a number would substitute its own rule for the corpus's. Who asserts it: § 107.37(b) names only the subject of the prohibition, "No person", and nobody whose determination settles the hazard, so assertedBy is the caller (0025).

entries.name: A covered structure or stationary vehicle provides reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft
entries.evidence: (b) Located under a covered structure or inside a stationary vehicle that can provide reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft.
entries.note: The standard qualifies the covered-structure exception; the exception itself is computable once it is asserted. The assertion is asserted and withheld for each of a covered structure and a stationary vehicle, attributed and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent. Split out rather than reclassifying over-human-beings, which states a further case that needs no judgement. Who asserts it: § 107.39 names the subject of the prohibition, "No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft over a human being", and the human being protected, and nobody whose determination settles the protection, so assertedBy is the caller (0025).

entries.name: Operation over a human being
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft over a human being unless that human being is: (a) Directly participating in the operation of the small unmanned aircraft; or (b) Located under a covered structure or inside a stationary vehicle that can provide reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft.
entries.note: Two causes, not one: the two exceptions this version states go opposite ways. (a) is direct-participation, a gap — "directly participating" is undefined and the exception turns entirely on it; (b) is reasonable-protection, an assertion, because "from a falling small unmanned aircraft" states the measure in the same constituent (0010). There is no subpart D of operational categories at this date and nothing to defer to. The evidence is the whole section, including both limbs of (b) — a covered structure and a stationary vehicle. The note this replaces said "One cause, not two", counting runtime reasons before (a)'s term had been read.

entries.name: A human being is directly participating in the operation
entries.evidence: (a) Directly participating in the operation of the small unmanned aircraft; or

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define "directly participating", and the term carries the whole of the § 107.39 exception it states: whether the aircraft may be flown over a person turns on it. "In the operation of the small unmanned aircraft" states what the participation is in, not how direct it must be, and no determination is vested in anybody.

entries.note: Gate 1 passes, gate 2 does not fire, and gate 3's first arm does not fire, so the procedure returns a gap. The same term delimits who must be briefed under § 107.49(b), and participant-briefing depends on this entry for that reason; the locator names § 107.39 alone because check-locators-section.py reads one section per citation, so an entry cannot cite two — a limit of the grammar rather than of the rule, stated where the claim is made. Compare § 107.39(b), whose "reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft" states its measure and is an assertion: two paragraphs of one sentence go opposite ways, and whose fact it is — a third party's, in both — is not what decides it. Found by 0010's re-derivation; trial 1's undefined-term sweep recorded this term against over-human-beings only and missed the § 107.49(b) instance.

entries.name: Reducing the anti-collision lighting intensity is in the interest of safety
entries.evidence: The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so.
entries.note: The corpus delegates the judgement and names its decider in the same breath: "if he or she determines". At this date the clause sits in § 107.29(b) alone and it grants the permission without bounding it: there is no "but may not extinguish". Amendment 107-8 both repeats the clause into § 107.29(a)(2) and adds that bound, so the consuming rule gains a computable constraint the earlier text does not state. This is the example method.md and corpus-map.md both cite for kind: assertion, and it had no entry of its own until #26.

entries.name: Anti-collision lighting during civil twilight
entries.evidence: (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system during periods of civil twilight unless the small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so.
entries.note: Fitted and unfitted, for civil twilight only — this version requires no lighting at night, because it forbids night operation outright. Visible for at least 3 statute miles. Whether reducing the intensity is in the interest of safety is the remote pilot in command's determination and is its own entry, intensity-reduction-in-interest-of-safety. This version states no flash-rate requirement, so there is no flash-rate-sufficient entry.

entries.name: Visual line of sight is maintained
entries.evidence: (a) With vision that is unaided by any device other than corrective lenses, the remote pilot in command, the visual observer (if one is used), and the person manipulating the flight control of the small unmanned aircraft system must be able to see the unmanned aircraft throughout the entire flight in order to: (1) Know the unmanned aircraft's location; (2) Determine the unmanned aircraft's attitude, altitude, and direction of flight; (3) Observe the airspace for other air traffic or hazards; and (4) Determine that the unmanned aircraft does not endanger the life or property of another. (b) Throughout the entire flight of the small unmanned aircraft, the ability described in paragraph (a) of this section must be exercised by either: (1) The remote pilot in command and the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system; or (2) A visual observer.

crossReferences.cites: the ability described in paragraph (a) of this section

entries.note: (b) states the two permitted combinations and the evidence covers both: the remote pilot in command together with the person manipulating the flight controls, or a visual observer — and neither. Given the assertion, that is a membership test against a fixed pair of combinations, which is computable, and it is what survives the split. The note this replaces said "whether anyone could in fact see the aircraft is not computable. The engine demands the assertion and records who made it" while the entry stayed kind: operation, so the assertion it described was recorded nowhere. It is unaided-visual-contact, and this entry depends on it (0010).

entries.name: The aircraft can be seen unaided throughout the entire flight, for the four stated purposes
entries.evidence: (a) With vision that is unaided by any device other than corrective lenses, the remote pilot in command, the visual observer (if one is used), and the person manipulating the flight control of the small unmanned aircraft system must be able to see the unmanned aircraft throughout the entire flight in order to: (1) Know the unmanned aircraft's location; (2) Determine the unmanned aircraft's attitude, altitude, and direction of flight; (3) Observe the airspace for other air traffic or hazards; and (4) Determine that the unmanned aircraft does not endanger the life or property of another.
entries.note: Gate 3's first arm fires on the plainest measure in this corpus. § 107.31(a) states an open ability — "must be able to see the unmanned aircraft throughout the entire flight" — and fixes what it is measured against in the same constituent, with "in order to:" and four enumerated purposes. That is the "sufficient to avoid a collision" construction with four adjuncts instead of one. § 107.31(a)(4)'s "endanger the life or property of another" sits inside that measure and is not a second open term: § 107.31 does not prohibit endangering, it requires the ability to see well enough to determine. The assertion is asserted and withheld for each named person, attributed and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent; the corpus states no distance, so no figure is evidenced. Split out of visual-line-of-sight, which keeps § 107.31(b)'s two permitted combinations — 0005's rule that a standard is its own entry and the rule that consumes it depends on it. Decided in 0010.

entries.name: Visual observer requirements, when one is used
entries.evidence: If a visual observer is used during the aircraft operation, all of the following requirements must be met: (a) The remote pilot in command, the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system, and the visual observer must maintain effective communication with each other at all times. (b) The remote pilot in command must ensure that the visual observer is able to see the unmanned aircraft in the manner specified in § 107.31. (c) The remote pilot in command, the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system, and the visual observer must coordinate to do the following: (1) Scan the airspace where the small unmanned aircraft is operating for any potential collision hazard; and (2) Maintain awareness of the position of the small unmanned aircraft through direct visual observation.
entries.note: What survives the split is (b) and the condition of application: if a visual observer is used, the remote pilot in command must ensure the observer can see the aircraft in the manner § 107.31 specifies — computable once unaided-visual-contact is asserted, reached through visual-line-of-sight. (a) is effective-communication, a gap; (c) is observer-coordination, an assertion. The section's three requirements do not share one verdict, which is what 0010 decides. § 107.33(b)'s "in the manner specified in § 107.31" is declared in crossReferences and resolves to visual-line-of-sight, the entry that states § 107.31 whole; it is the same edge as dependsOn. An earlier sentence here said the words were outside check-map.py's pointer list and nothing demanded a declaration; the manifest's pointerPhrases now detect "§ 107.31" (0026), so that was no longer true.

entries.name: Effective communication is maintained among the three named persons
entries.evidence: (a) The remote pilot in command, the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system, and the visual observer must maintain effective communication with each other at all times.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define "effective", and the term carries the whole of § 107.33(a). The paragraph states no measure for it in its own constituent — "with each other at all times" fixes between whom and when, not what effectiveness is measured against — and vests the determination in nobody: it is an obligation on three named persons, not a judgement the corpus gives them.

entries.note: Gate 1 passes: applying the paragraph requires fixing a degree the corpus did not fix. Gate 2 does not fire — § 107.3 does not define the term and no corpus is named for it. Gate 3's first arm does not fire, so the procedure returns a gap: the same shape as well-clear, prominent-objects and moving-vehicle-operation's "sparsely populated area". That the operator is the only person who could answer the question is not what gate 3 asks. An operator who asserts that communication was effective has asserted a conclusion the engine cannot check and that the corpus gave it no warrant to delegate; 0008 § 2 rules that where a term's determinacy rests on knowledge outside the corpus, that belief is fate: decision with a record, never a kind. Split out of visual-observer-conditions (0010).

entries.name: The three named persons coordinate to scan the airspace and maintain awareness
entries.evidence: (c) The remote pilot in command, the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system, and the visual observer must coordinate to do the following: (1) Scan the airspace where the small unmanned aircraft is operating for any potential collision hazard; and (2) Maintain awareness of the position of the small unmanned aircraft through direct visual observation.
entries.note: Gate 3's first arm fires: "must coordinate" is followed in the same constituent by "to do the following:" and a closed two-item enumeration — scan the airspace for any potential collision hazard, and maintain awareness of the position through direct visual observation. The infinitival adjunct states what the coordination is for exactly as "to avoid a collision" states what the flash rate is for. "Maintain awareness" is inside that enumeration and is not a second open term, and "through direct visual observation" fixes its means. The assertion is asserted and withheld, attributed to the three named persons and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent. Split out of visual-observer-conditions (0010).

entries.name: Preflight familiarization, inspection and actions
entries.evidence: Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must: (a) Assess the operating environment, considering risks to persons and property in the immediate vicinity both on the surface and in the air. This assessment must include: (1) Local weather conditions; (2) Local airspace and any flight restrictions; (3) The location of persons and property on the surface; and (4) Other ground hazards. (b) Ensure that all persons directly participating in the small unmanned aircraft operation are informed about the operating conditions, emergency procedures, contingency procedures, roles and responsibilities, and potential hazards; (c) Ensure that all control links between ground control station and the small unmanned aircraft are working properly; (d) If the small unmanned aircraft is powered, ensure that there is enough available power for the small unmanned aircraft system to operate for the intended operational time; and (e) Ensure that any object attached or carried by the small unmanned aircraft is secure and does not adversely affect the flight characteristics or controllability of the aircraft.
entries.note: Five obligations in this text, and they do not share one verdict: (a), (b) and (d) are assertions, (c) is a gap, and (e) is one of each — preflight-risk-assessment, participant-briefing, control-links-working, sufficient-available-power, attached-object-secure and attached-object-no-adverse-effect. The note this replaces said "Five obligations, all assertions about what a person did", which is wrong twice over: three of them are about equipment rather than conduct, and two state no measure at all and are gaps (0010). Each obligation asserted and unasserted. What is left here is the conjunction: prior to flight the remote pilot in command must do all of them. § 107.49 has no paragraph (f) at this date.

entries.name: The operating environment has been assessed against the stated risks
entries.evidence: (a) Assess the operating environment, considering risks to persons and property in the immediate vicinity both on the surface and in the air. This assessment must include: (1) Local weather conditions; (2) Local airspace and any flight restrictions; (3) The location of persons and property on the surface; and (4) Other ground hazards.
entries.note: Gate 3's first arm fires twice over: "Assess the operating environment" is qualified in its own constituent by "considering risks to persons and property in the immediate vicinity both on the surface and in the air" — what the assessment is measured against — and then by a closed four-item list of what it must include. The bearer is named in the section's lead-in, "Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must:", and is who asserts it (assertedBy, 0025). The limit, stated where the claim is made: the measure itself carries an open degree, "immediate vicinity", and gate 3 does not ask whether a stated measure is itself determinate. A measure that needs a measure is a shape 0008's procedure cannot see; 0010 records it rather than deciding it.

entries.name: The directly participating persons have been informed of the five stated matters
entries.evidence: (b) Ensure that all persons directly participating in the small unmanned aircraft operation are informed about the operating conditions, emergency procedures, contingency procedures, roles and responsibilities, and potential hazards;
entries.note: "Informed about" is fixed by the set stated in the same constituent — operating conditions, emergency procedures, contingency procedures, roles and responsibilities, and potential hazards — which is gate 3's second arm, the delegated choice among values the corpus fixes ("either thrice or four times"), and the set is quotable from this entry's own evidence. The audience is not fixed: "all persons directly participating" is the same undefined term as § 107.39(a), which is direct-participation, a gap, and this entry depends on it. One paragraph, two open terms, two verdicts — which is the sharpest instance of what 0010 decides. Who asserts it is named in § 107.49's lead-in, "Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must:" (assertedBy, 0025).

entries.name: The control links are working properly
entries.evidence: (c) Ensure that all control links between ground control station and the small unmanned aircraft are working properly;

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define "working properly", and the term carries the whole obligation. § 107.49(c) states no measure for it in its own constituent — "between ground control station and the small unmanned aircraft" identifies which links, not what properly is measured against — and vests the determination in nobody.

entries.note: Gate 3 returns a gap, the same answer as effective-communication, prominent-objects and well-clear. That the remote pilot in command is the only person who could answer it is not gate 3's question (0008 § 2). Split out of preflight-actions (0010).

entries.name: There is enough available power for the intended operational time
entries.evidence: (d) If the small unmanned aircraft is powered, ensure that there is enough available power for the small unmanned aircraft system to operate for the intended operational time; and
entries.note: "Enough available power" is followed in its own constituent by "for the small unmanned aircraft system to operate for the intended operational time" — an infinitival adjunct on enough, the same construction as "a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision". Gate 3's first arm fires. The intended operational time is an ordinary caller-supplied parameter that gate 1 stops and that gets no entry of its own, as corpus-map.md rules for airspace-authorized's airspace class. Split out of preflight-actions (0010). Who asserts it is named in § 107.49's lead-in, "Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must:" (assertedBy, 0025).

entries.name: An attached or carried object is secure
entries.evidence: Ensure that any object attached or carried by the small unmanned aircraft is secure

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define "secure", and § 107.49(e) states no measure for it. The second conjunct — "and does not adversely affect the flight characteristics or controllability of the aircraft" — is a coordinate predicate of the same copula, not the measure of the first.

entries.note: 0008 § 2 rules that a coordinate conjunct is a second obligation rather than a measure, which is exactly how "must give way" was refused as the measure of "well clear". So § 107.49(e) is two entries with opposite verdicts, this one and attached-object-no-adverse-effect. The limit, stated where the claim is made: a reader could take the second conjunct as a gloss on the first — secure enough not to affect the flight — and 0005 refused to put one sentence under two ids when it declined to split must-play-whole-throw. The nearer precedent is followed instead: right-of-way and well-clear are one sentence under two ids for precisely this reason (0010).

entries.name: An attached or carried object does not adversely affect flight characteristics or controllability
entries.evidence: does not adversely affect the flight characteristics or controllability of the aircraft
entries.note: "Adversely affect" states what it is measured against in its own constituent and enumerates it: the flight characteristics or controllability of the aircraft. Gate 3's first arm fires. Split from attached-object-secure, whose conjunct states no measure (0010). Who asserts it is named in § 107.49's lead-in, "Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must:" (assertedBy, 0025).

entries.name: Certificate of waiver: issuance, and deviation under it
entries.evidence: (a) The Administrator may issue a certificate of waiver authorizing a deviation from any regulation specified in § 107.205 if the Administrator finds that a proposed small UAS operation can safely be conducted under the terms of that certificate of waiver. (b) A request for a certificate of waiver must contain a complete description of the proposed operation and justification that establishes that the operation can safely be conducted under the terms of a certificate of waiver. (c) The Administrator may prescribe additional limitations that the Administrator considers necessary. (d) A person who receives a certificate of waiver issued under this section: (1) May deviate from the regulations of this part to the extent specified in the certificate of waiver; and (2) Must comply with any conditions or limitations that are specified in the certificate of waiver.
entries.note: Out of scope: this map reads twelve sections of subpart B, and § 107.200 is in subpart D, which at this date is "Subpart D - Waivers" (the operational categories the 2026 text puts in subpart D did not exist yet, and waivers moved to subpart E). It is an entry rather than an omission because rules inside the slice reach it through § 107.205, which lists the regulations a certificate issued pursuant to it may authorize deviation from (waivable-regulations, which (a) points at: "specified in § 107.205"). Unlike the 2026 map, no rule in the slice names § 107.200 itself: § 107.29 has no paragraph (d) at this date, so there is no night-waiver-bar or night-waiver-termination. Nothing under the section is worked: whether to issue is the Administrator's finding under (a), and what a holder may do is "to the extent specified in the certificate of waiver" under (d), subject to conditions and limitations the certificate states and the corpus does not. The evidence is the whole section, so that the out-of-scope verdict covers the finding, the request, the additional limitations and the holder's deviation alike. The text is identical to § 107.200 at 2026-01-01 (#61, 0021).

entries.name: Regulations a certificate of waiver may authorize deviation from
entries.evidence: A certificate of waiver issued pursuant to § 107.200 may authorize a deviation from the following regulations of this part: (a) Section 107.25 - Operation from a moving vehicle or aircraft. However, no waiver of this provision will be issued to allow the carriage of property of another by aircraft for compensation or hire. (b) Section 107.29 - Daylight operation. (c) Section 107.31 - Visual line of sight aircraft operation. However, no waiver of this provision will be issued to allow the carriage of property of another by aircraft for compensation or hire. (d) Section 107.33 - Visual observer. (e) Section 107.35 - Operation of multiple small unmanned aircraft systems. (f) Section 107.37(a) - Yielding the right of way. (g) Section 107.39 - Operation over people. (h) Section 107.41 - Operation in certain airspace. (i) Section 107.51 - Operating limitations for small unmanned aircraft.

crossReferences.unmapped: § 107.51's introductory text, "must comply with all of the following operating limitations", has no entry in this map, so the three items above state (a) to (d) and not the sentence that binds them together. It is the gap the 2026 map's blind second mapping closed with operating-limitations, and it is left to the blind second mapping this map owes.

entries.note: Out of scope for the same reason as waiver-policy, and the gate every waivable rule in this map names in suspendedBy: a rule a certificate of waiver authorizes deviation from is unreachable while the waiver is held. The map records the edge and not the condition (0003); whether a waiver is held and what it authorizes deviation from is a fact about an instrument the Administrator issued, which the caller states and the engine never infers in either direction (0021). The list is read from the 2020-01-01 text, not carried from the 2026 map, and differs from it in two places: (b) lists "Section 107.29" whole rather than "Section 107.29(a)(2) and (b)", and there is no (j), because § 107.145 did not exist. The item separator at this date is " - ", not an em dash. The edges follow the list paragraph by paragraph, judged by what each entry's locator states: (a) § 107.25 — moving-vehicle-operation, which at this date states both limbs of the section. (b) § 107.29, the whole section — night-operation ((a)), anti-collision-lighting and intensity-reduction-in-interest-of-safety ((b)), civil-twilight-operation ((b)-(c)), civil-twilight-window ((c)(1)-(2)) and civil-twilight-alaska ((c)(3)); the definitional values are included because the listed regulation is the section that states them, as for § 107.51. night-operation is the entry the 2026 map leaves out, and here it is the plainest edge: the rule is "No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system during night" and the waiver list names its section. That it declines on its own account (definedElsewhere, § 1.1) does not change what suspends it. (c) § 107.31 — visual-line-of-sight, unaided-visual-contact. (d) § 107.33 — visual-observer-conditions, effective-communication, observer-coordination. (e) § 107.35 — single-aircraft. (f) § 107.37(a) — right-of-way, well-clear; not collision-hazard-proximity, which is (b). (g) § 107.39 — over-human-beings, direct-participation, reasonable-protection. (h) § 107.41 — airspace-authorized. (i) § 107.51, the whole section — speed-limit, altitude-limit, visibility-minimum, cloud-clearance, speed-within-limit, altitude-within-limit, weather-minimums-met, prominent-objects. Not suspended: restricted-area-permitted (§ 107.45), hazardous-material (§ 107.36), collision-hazard-proximity (§ 107.37(b)) and the seven § 107.49 entries; none is listed. Each "Section 107.xx" pointer resolves to the entry at the level of the listed regulation: the whole section or paragraph where one entry states it. "Section 107.29" is declared twice, to night-operation and civil-twilight-operation, because no one entry states the whole section and those two together do. "Section 107.51" is declared four times: to speed-within-limit, altitude-within-limit and weather-minimums-met, which together state (a) to (d), and once unmapped, because this map has no entry for § 107.51's introductory text (the 2026 map's operating-limitations, which only its blind second mapping found); that gap is left to the blind second mapping this map owes. The edges above reach further than those resolutions, to every entry inside the listed regulation. The provisos in (a) and (c), "no waiver of this provision will be issued to allow the carriage of property of another by aircraft for compensation or hire", bound what the Administrator will issue, and are not evaluated. They do not amend § 107.25(b) or § 107.31; they mean no waiver of either will be issued that allows that carriage, so the edges on moving-vehicle-operation, visual-line-of-sight and unaided-visual-contact reach further than an issued waiver can. That costs a decline, not a wrong answer: a holder deviates only "to the extent specified in the certificate of waiver" (§ 107.200(d)(1)), and while the caller states a waiver is held the entry answers OutsideCurrentScope rather than a verdict. No suspended entry's own note repeats this judgement; it is recorded here, once.
